Q: Is reviewing by sight only a good use of Claude Code to write code? A:

I review the code by sight only, which very obviously becomes overwhelming, and I just "Accept All" after a while.

This is where I see you got into trouble.

Don't give in to this temptation. You must not use AI to write more code than you can review thoroughly.

Developing code is always time-consuming. "Overwhelming" is the phrase you used. But it's not the keystrokes that take the most time. It's developing your understanding of the code. It's going through it in your head again and again until you are confident that it's doing the job you want it to do, and it's efficient, secure, maintainable, has good style, fits your architecture, supports testing, and all the other things you need to do to make professional software.

If you skip these steps, you're cheating yourself, and you're cheating your employer.

I read a post by a developer using Claude to write some software last year.

Now, I didn't review any of the code [the LLM] generated - not because I didn't want to, but because the sheer volume of code it was generating overwhelmed me (first red flag).

Sound familiar?

Of course it was hard to verify and then to maintain the code that he had never reviewed. He ended up having to spend practically as much time to learn the code as if he had written it manually himself.

In his conclusion, he wrote:

Another funny thing - when the entire app was built in under two hours with barely any input from me, I felt… oddly depressed. But after spending two weeks cleaning things up, making the app actually work, I felt grounded again. Like I’d reclaimed something.

What he reclaimed, I think, was ownership of his code. I mean, after spending time with it properly, he felt he had done his job, and he felt ownership—both the credit for having done it, and the responsibility for maintaining it.

I believe professional people want to feel ownership of their work. AI tries to steal this from you, and you must maintain discipline to use it only as a tool, not as the primary developer.

What do I mean by using it as a tool?

Compare with a much simpler tool: code completion. This has been a feature of code editors for decades, and people are used to it. (Let me tell you as a person who started his career writing X11/Motif code in vi: you probably don't appreciate how tedious it is to try to remember hundreds of 30-character camel-cased method names and have to correct your typos when you use a non-smart editor.)

But code completion doesn't write the code for you. It doesn't design code or choose the functions. It only replaces the part that is the most rote for you, like filling in 27 of the 30 characters of the method name you want.

Using AI should be similar, in my opinion. Use it to generate boilerplate code. You won't learn anything new by writing an API handler for the 500th time. Let the AI do the parts that you could do in your sleep, and would only take you longer.

Or use it as a code reviewer. Write the code yourself, and then let the AI analyze it and make suggestions. You don't have to take all of its suggestions.

Or use the AI to generate small bits of code, like usage of a specific function, or adding required comment blocks. For example, I always found Doxygen or Swagger was kind of fiddly and easy to get wrong, and I would have loved to use a tool to generate properly-formed comment blocks, at least to start.

Q: How should I partition a memory region returned by mmap() into allocator blocks? A:

Yes, your approach is correct. mmap() returns one contiguous memory region, and placing block headers inside that region is how most custom allocators work. Just use byte-wise pointer arithmetic (char * or uint8_t *) and make sure each block is aligned (typically to alignof(max_align_t) or 16 bytes) before creating the next header.
